assessmentSummary.identity: One Jump Rope Bounce repetition is one rope revolution with a low simultaneous bilateral takeoff and landing on a clean, level, non-slip surface while a hand-held rope passes under both feet. The basic-bounce card is a low-amplitude two-foot rope rhythm task, not mimed jumping, alternating-foot skipping, boxer step, single-leg skipping, double-under, weighted-rope work, conditioning intervals, power jumping, or a landing assessment.
currentCardFindings: Source 49, Jump Rope Easy Bounce, was deterministically consolidated into the jump-rope-bounce survivor. Its old variant is an archived source skeleton and must remain traceable rather than being silently selectable.
Source labels such as easy and low describe candidate amplitude, pace, contacts, and duration. They do not establish participant skill, age, readiness, clinical eligibility, or a universal dose.

Four direct YouTube candidates returned oEmbed metadata on 2026-08-09. Playback, current availability, embedding, exact mechanics, captions, accessibility, quality, and approval remain human-review work.

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Select only when the exact two-foot rope-pass contract, rope length and handle condition, clean level non-slip surface, ceiling and lateral clearance, footwear or approved bare-foot policy, contact budget, symptoms, communication, staffing, and downstream running, jumping, landing, and calf exposure fit. Recompute selection, fatigue, impact, duration, logistics, substitution, persistence, and rendering after any change.

calibrationEvidence.basis: Direct jump-rope footwear and alternating-foot biomechanics studies, a professional supervised-training standard, the merged Source 49 lineage, and comparison with low pogos, rope power singles, alternating-foot rope skipping, boxer step, double-under, and interval work.
calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: The studies do not establish a universal cadence, amplitude, contact ceiling, dose, recovery interval, participant threshold, outcome, or Vortex score. Human review is required for every score, relationship, and video.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Stand on a clean, level, non-slip surface with a correctly sized unweighted jump rope held in both hands. Rotate the rope with the hands and wrists so it passes under both feet once. Make one low simultaneous bilateral takeoff, clear the rope, and land quietly on both feet before the next pass. One rope revolution with one bilateral takeoff and landing is one repetition. Record valid passes, misses, actual contact count, cadence, rope type, surface, footwear, symptoms, and rest. Alternating-foot, boxer, single-leg, double-under, mimed, weighted-rope, high-output, interval, assessment, and other changed tasks require their own reviewed variant or definition.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Jump-Rope-Specific Footwear Selection on Lower Extremity Biomechanics
claims: The study distinguishes one- and two-leg jump-rope landing conditions.
Vortex defines this candidate as the simultaneous bilateral basic-bounce condition only.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Barefoot and Shod Conditions on the Kinematics and Kinetics of the Lower Extremities in Alternating Jump Rope Skipping
claims: Alternating jump-rope skipping is a separately studied task.
Alternating-foot, boxer-step, and single-leg patterns remain separate variants or definitions rather than annotations.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Jump-Rope-Specific Footwear Selection on Lower Extremity Biomechanics
claims: The study measured plantar pressure and lower-extremity muscle activity during jump rope.
The card records foot, ankle, calf, knee, hip, trunk, shoulder, and wrist roles without claiming isolated activation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Barefoot and Shod Conditions on the Kinematics and Kinetics of the Lower Extremities in Alternating Jump Rope Skipping
claims: Ankle and metatarsophalangeal kinematics and kinetics are relevant during alternating rope skipping.
Rope clearance, bilateral contacts, low amplitude, and hand-driven rope rotation are explicit observable mechanics for this candidate.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Jump-Rope-Specific Footwear Selection on Lower Extremity Biomechanics
claims: One- and two-leg landing conditions had different measured loading characteristics.
Candidate scores describe exercise complexity and physical demand only, never a person's skill or age.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Jump-Rope-Specific Footwear Selection on Lower Extremity Biomechanics
claims: Repeated jump rope produces measured ground-reaction force, plantar-pressure, and muscle-activity exposure.
The card counts valid contacts and records surface, footwear, cadence, misses, symptoms, and overlapping impact instead of asserting a universal recovery time.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Safe environment, instruction, supervision, and progressive exposure are relevant to supervised exercise.
Vortex requires rope, clearance, surface, visibility, communication, and exit checks without demographic classification.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Jump-Rope-Specific Footwear Selection on Lower Extremity Biomechanics
claims: The laboratory task does not establish a universal workout dose.
Candidate bout and contact proposals remain review-only and stop before repeated-contact quality declines.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Barefoot and Shod Conditions on the Kinematics and Kinetics of the Lower Extremities in Alternating Jump Rope Skipping
claims: Rope skipping has distinct landing and lower-limb phases.
Vortex cues a low bilateral pass, quiet landing, wrist-driven rope rotation, and counted valid passes without prescribing a clinical technique.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Supervision and safe training conditions should be matched to the task and setting.
Stop for pain, new neurologic or circulation symptoms, repeated trips, unsafe clearance, loud or uncontrolled contacts, or inability to communicate.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Jump-Rope-Specific Footwear Selection on Lower Extremity Biomechanics
claims: Footwear and landing condition changed measured jump-rope loading characteristics.
Any change of footwear, landing pattern, amplitude, cadence, rope type, surface, or dose requires revalidation of exposure and selection.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Instruction and supervision are relevant safeguards for resistance and conditioning activity.
Athlete support uses plain cues, a clear stop signal, and an option to stop rather than chase continuous passes.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Jump-Rope-Specific Footwear Selection on Lower Extremity Biomechanics
claims: The study measured differences between landing conditions.
Coaches observe rope clearance, bilateral contact pattern, amplitude, surface, footwear, contact sound, trips, symptoms, and actual passes without diagnosing impairment.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Instruction and supervised progression should be matched to the task and setting.
Captions, transcript, still sequence, visual station markers, live verbal cueing, and a different reviewed task remain candidate supports; a mimed task is not automatically equivalent.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Barefoot and Shod Conditions on the Kinematics and Kinetics of the Lower Extremities in Alternating Jump Rope Skipping
claims: Alternating jump-rope skipping differs from bilateral basic bouncing in lower-extremity mechanics.
The alternate review explicitly separates contact pattern, rope requirement, amplitude, pace, external load, and interval intent.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Instruction and supervision need task-specific review.
